prompt_cache.$comment: Applied to the input side of per-token rates only. A per-outcome product bills a completed unit of work, so the buyer's price does not move with cacheability.
prompt_cache.basis: measured across 969 local Claude Code transcripts and 50,279 API calls: 98.2% of context tokens were served from cache, 1.8% written to it, and a negligible share billed fresh. Cache reads bill at a tenth of the input rate and writes at 1.25 times it, so input costs 12.07% of the list rate.
prompt_cache.not_applied: Batch processing at 50% and committed-spend discounts, reported to average 28% on negotiated enterprise agreements, are available on several of these providers and are not applied.

per_task.billing: per unit of work completed, not per token
per_task.tokens_per_task_basis: median session measured across 969 local Claude Code transcripts and 50,279 API calls: 981,000 context tokens and 4,000 output tokens. Sessions run 349:1 input to output, and 98.2% of context is cache reads.
per_task.note: These products price a completed unit of work rather than a token. Each is converted to a per-million-token equivalent by dividing its rate by its tokens_per_task. Where a vendor publishes a range, the lowest figure is used, and each tokens_per_task is set at the generous end of the plausible range, so every equivalent rate here is the cheapest defensible reading.

unpriced.note: Sierra, Decagon and Ada advertise per-outcome pricing without publishing a rate; contracts are reported at $50,000 to $600,000 a year. ServiceNow Now Assist bills per assist, 25 for a small generative task and 150 for a large agentic action, with no published price per assist. Workday Illuminate includes Flex Credits in the subscription with no published per-agent rate.

google_vertex.billing: per endpoint instance hour plus a per-model container fee. No per-token tier for open weights.
google_vertex.derivation: a4-highgpu-8g at $16.11/GPU-hour, divided by modelled serving throughput, divided again by 40% endpoint utilisation
google_vertex.excluded: per-model container fee, published per Marketplace listing. Google's real cost is higher than shown.
google_vertex.absent_openai: Vertex Model Garden carries no OpenAI proprietary models. Google cannot reach the Luna price or accuracy, so its Max case stays on open weights with best-of-three.

azure_foundry.note: Foundry Agent Service charges nothing to create or run an agent, but it is a CONTROL PLANE, not a runtime. Microsoft bills model tokens, search services, storage and compute invoked by the agent. Agent code and tools run on Azure Container Apps at $0.000024/vCPU-second and $0.000003/GiB-second. Azure compute is DEARER than AgentCore Runtime, not free.

aws_agentcore.note: Monthly charge against an accumulating balance. This is why the AWS memory line compounds, and it is the largest single driver of our AWS advantage. Check every run.

azure_assembled.sizing: 300M records with vectors needs roughly 12 partitions x 2 replicas of AI Search S3 at $981.12 per search unit per month, about $282K/yr. AI Search bills per unit-hour regardless of query volume.
azure_assembled.note: Infrastructure comparison only. AgentCore Memory performs extraction and consolidation a customer assembling Cosmos DB and AI Search would build.

google_agent_engine.note: No monthly accrual, so this line does not compound.

aws_cloudwatch.note: Volume tiers exist ($0.50 to 10TB, then $0.25, $0.10, $0.05) but apply only to AWS vended logs. Agent payload arrives via PutLogEvents and bills flat.

gpt-5.6-luna.note: OpenAI published no SWE-bench Verified score for the GPT-5.6 family. Published instead: SWE-bench Pro 62.7%, Terminal-Bench 2.1 84.7%, Coding Agent Index 75, Intelligence Index 51. On SWE-bench Pro, Luna leads DeepSeek V4 Pro at 55.4% and MiniMax M3 at 59.0%, and V4 Pro scores 80.6% on Verified, so 88 is a reasoned placement rather than a measurement. One aggregator returns 96/92/86/67 for Luna on Verified, which is a garbled table and must not be used. Re-attempt every run.

serving_throughput.mixed_length_haircut_note: Midpoint of the 1.5x to 2x degradation this block's own note warns of for mixed sequence lengths. Applied to the Akka side of the API vs Akka comparison so the modelled throughput is not the optimistic figure. Not applied to the other tabs, whose figures predate it.
serving_throughput.note: First-principles from FLOPs and HBM bandwidth. Never benchmarked. Our own analysis warned mixed sequence lengths land 1.5-2x worse. Benchmarking retires the largest single uncertainty in the model.

peak_factor.note: Measured for coding workloads across 44M requests in Microsoft's Azure inference traces. Measured at pooled scale, so a single tenant's true peak is higher.

akka_model.note_min_nodes: residency floor: both base models resident with HA across two zones

capacity_projection.note: Published as a commitment. Compounded modelled gain is 3.0x; we publish roughly half.

cpu_storage.model: declining per 5T block, independent of GPU spend and identical on every cloud
cpu_storage.note: Follows deployed agents and end-user traffic, not GPU spend. Marginal cost per block: $100K, $87K, $76K, $67K, $59K, reaching the $15K floor around the fortieth block.
cpu_storage.corrected_from: 12.5% of GPU spend tapering to 7%. See corrections log.

corrections.what: Azure agent hosting and memory were understated by roughly $2.3M at 5T
corrections.why_wrong: Foundry Agent Service advertises no charge to run an agent. That was read as no compute cost. The service is a control plane; the agent's own code and tools run on Azure compute billed separately, and every retrieval hits AI Search which bills per unit-hour whether or not it serves.
corrections.how_found: A reviewer asked why a free runtime at that scale made commercial sense. It did not.
corrections.lesson: When a provider advertises no charge for a component, find where the work actually runs before recording a zero. A zero on a line that must consume resources is a signal to look harder, not a finding.
corrections.effect: Azure High moved from $4.76M to $7.10M at 5T. The AWS-versus-Azure gap narrowed from $3.33M to $985K.

corrections.what: Compute and storage were priced as a share of GPU spend
corrections.was: 12.5% of the GPU line, tapering to 7% with volume
corrections.now: a declining schedule per 5T block: $100K for the first, decaying toward a $15K floor, with a $50K minimum
corrections.why_wrong: Tying the line to GPU spend made it rise on clouds with dearer GPUs. At 5T it read $90K on AWS but $273K on Google for identical work, which inflated Google by $173K for no reason other than its GPU rate.
corrections.how_found: A per-provider cost decomposition showed compute and storage moving with the GPU rate when they depend on agents and traffic.
corrections.lesson: Price a line on what actually drives it. A coefficient tied to another line inherits that line's variance whether or not the causation exists.
corrections.effect: Compute and storage are now identical on all three clouds. Akka on Google fell from $4.94M to $4.60M at 5T, on Azure from $3.51M to $3.33M, and rose slightly on AWS from $1.65M to $1.67M.

techniques.name: Specialist models for routine work

techniques.name: Remembering what you asked before
techniques.desc: Agents repeat the same instructions every turn. Reading them back costs a fraction of reading them fresh.

techniques.name: Guessing ahead while writing
techniques.desc: A small fast model guesses the next words and the big model checks them together.

techniques.name: Running unattended work off-peak
techniques.desc: Anything with nobody waiting runs later, on machines that would sit idle.
